task: This is a synthetic writing exercise. Using these fictional reporting notes, write a newspaper reported feature for general readers. Draw only on the supplied notes; do not invent additional reported events, scenes, or quotations. Write from this reporting snapshot as of March 31, 2025. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: Nexus Semiconductor broke ground on a chip fabrication plant in Sonoran Valley, Arizona, in January 2025; the facility will consume up to 14 million liters of ultra-pure water per day at full production.
Sonoran Valley receives an average of 28 centimeters of rainfall per year and relies on Colorado River water allocations that have been reduced three times since 2019.

The state's water allocation to the new facility is contingent on Nexus achieving 80% water recycling efficiency within two years of full production — a target the company says it is designed to meet.

Water policy researcher Dr. Mira Espinoza of Sonoran University said: "The state is betting that new industrial users will be more efficient than legacy agriculture. Historically, that bet has sometimes not paid off."
Local alfalfa farmer Jack Dunbar, 64, has farmed 3,200 acres in Sonoran Valley for 38 years; his water allocation was reduced 18% in 2022 to help meet downstream Colorado River commitments.
Dunbar said: "I gave up water so the valley could survive. Now they're giving it to a chip factory. That's a choice somebody made. Nobody asked me."

Nexus's water management director, Dr. Sofia Reyes, said the facility uses a closed-loop ultra-pure water system that recycles 83% of water used in chip rinsing; the remainder is either evaporated or treated to municipal discharge standards.

Dr. Reyes said: "We are not a conventional industrial water user. Our economic output per liter of water consumed is higher than virtually any other use, including agriculture. That comparison matters in a scarcity context."
Dr. Espinoza said the value-per-unit-water argument is real but incomplete: it does not account for the cultural and food security value of agricultural water rights, which predate the facility.
The facility will employ 2,400 people at wages averaging $78,000 per year; the county's median household income is $48,000.

Dunbar said he is not opposed to semiconductor manufacturing in principle but questions whether the desert Southwest is the right place: "We've been telling people for a decade that we don't have enough water. Now we're bringing in the biggest water user in the world."

Nexus's state permit requires quarterly water use reporting and grants regulators authority to reduce the company's allocation if recycling efficiency falls below 75%; the permit does not specify what happens to the facility if that reduction is imposed.
A state water official said the permit's recycling requirement is stricter than any previously applied to an industrial user in Arizona; the official declined to comment on enforcement precedent.
Dr. Espinoza said the recycling target is technically achievable but operationally challenging — chip facilities often run below target efficiency during ramp-up and maintenance periods.

Nexus has also signed an agreement to fund restoration of 4,200 acre-feet of Colorado River flows through a conservation-purchase program; critics say this is a small fraction of the facility's projected consumption.
Dunbar said he has talked to some of his neighbors about whether to sell their farms; two have sold to residential developers in the past year.

Dr. Reyes said the facility's location was chosen partly for its proximity to existing semiconductor supply chain partners in Phoenix; the water situation was a known risk that Nexus's engineers said they could manage.

State economic development officials said Nexus represents $6.8 billion in direct investment and will anchor a semiconductor cluster that could attract additional companies; water is a solvable engineering problem, they said, not a reason to forgo the investment.

Dr. Espinoza said the state's framing of water as a technical problem to be engineered around is itself part of the debate: "Scarcity is not only a technical problem. It is a question of who gets less."

Dunbar said he has reduced his alfalfa acreage by 600 acres in the past three years and is studying whether drip-irrigated specialty crops are viable on part of his land; he said the transition is expensive and uncertain.
